description: Redshift, Hubble's law, Big Bang evidence, and the mystery of dark matter and dark energy.
content_html:
The Expanding Universe

One of the most profound discoveries in science is that the universe is expanding. In the 1920s, astronomers began measuring the spectra of distant galaxies and noticed something remarkable: the absorption lines in almost every galaxy’s spectrum were shifted to longer, redder wavelengths. This redshift indicates that galaxies are moving away from us. The more distant a galaxy, the greater its redshift — and therefore the faster it is receding. This is not galaxies moving through space; it is space itself that is expanding, carrying galaxies apart like raisins in a rising dough.

The Redshift Formula

The relationship between observed wavelength shift and recession velocity is given by:

$$\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{v}{c}$$

where \(\Delta\lambda\) is the change in wavelength (observed minus rest wavelength), \(\lambda\) is the rest wavelength, \(v\) is the recession velocity of the galaxy, and \(c\) is the speed of light (3 × 10&sup8; m/s). A galaxy with \(\Delta\lambda / \lambda = 0.05\) is receding at 5% of the speed of light. This formula applies for velocities much less than \(c\); at very high redshifts (quasars, early universe), relativistic corrections are needed.

Key Fact

Redshift formula: \(\Delta\lambda / \lambda = v / c\). The numerator \(\Delta\lambda\) is the shift in wavelength; \(\lambda\) is the rest wavelength; \(v\) is the recession velocity; \(c\) is the speed of light. A positive \(\Delta\lambda\) means redshift (receding); a negative \(\Delta\lambda\) would mean blueshift (approaching, as with the Andromeda Galaxy).

Hubble’s Law

In 1929, Edwin Hubble published his finding that galaxy recession velocity is proportional to distance:

$$v = H_0 d$$

where \(v\) is the recession velocity in km/s, \(d\) is the distance in megaparsecs (Mpc), and \(H_0\) is the Hubble constant \(H_0 \approx 70\) km/s/Mpc. This means that a galaxy 100 Mpc away is receding at approximately 7,000 km/s. Hubble’s law implies that the universe had a beginning: running the expansion backwards gives an age for the universe of approximately \(1/H_0 \approx 13.8\) billion years. This is consistent with the independently measured ages of the oldest stars.

A galaxy has a spectral line normally at a rest wavelength of 500 nm observed at 510 nm.

Step 1 — Find velocity from redshift: \(\Delta\lambda = 510 - 500 = 10\) nm. \(v = c \times \Delta\lambda / \lambda = 3 \times 10^5 \text{ km/s} \times (10/500) = 6,000\) km/s.

Step 2 — Find distance from Hubble’s law: \(d = v / H_0 = 6,000 / 70 \approx 85.7\) Mpc.

The Big Bang Theory — Evidence

The Big Bang theory proposes that the universe began in an extremely hot, dense state approximately 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding and cooling ever since. Three key pieces of observational evidence support it:

  • Hubble’s law and galaxy redshifts — all galaxies (except local group members bound by gravity) are receding; the farther away, the faster. Running the expansion backwards implies a single origin point.
  • The cosmic microwave background (CMB) — in 1965, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered a faint, uniform cosmic microwave background radiation coming equally from all directions. Its temperature is approximately 2.7 K — the predicted cooled remnant of the hot early universe. The CMB could not have a competing explanation as a Steady State relic. Tiny temperature fluctuations (anisotropies) in the CMB, mapped by WMAP and the Planck satellite, reveal the seeds of the large-scale structure that grew into today’s galaxies.
  • Quasar distribution — quasars are found predominantly at high redshifts (great distances, early cosmic time). This shows the universe was different in the past — inconsistent with the Steady State model, which requires the universe to look the same at all epochs.

The Steady State theory, championed by Fred Hoyle, predicted that the universe would look the same at all epochs, with matter being continuously created to fill in the expanding gaps. The discovery of the CMB and the distribution of quasars decisively rejected this model.

Key Fact

Three key pieces of Big Bang evidence: (1) Galaxy redshifts and Hubble’s law — universe is expanding; (2) Cosmic microwave background at 2.7 K — cooled remnant of the hot early universe, detected uniformly from all directions; (3) Quasar distribution at high redshift — universe was different in the past.

Dark Matter

Observations of galactic rotation curves show that stars far from the galactic centre orbit much faster than the visible mass of the galaxy can account for. If only visible matter were present, orbital speeds should decrease with distance (like planets in the Solar System). Instead, they remain roughly constant — implying a large amount of unseen mass, called dark matter, distributed throughout the galactic halo. Dark matter cannot be detected electromagnetically: it does not emit, absorb or reflect light. Its nature remains unknown; candidates include weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) and axions. Dark matter accounts for approximately 27% of the total energy density of the universe.

Dark Energy and the Fate of the Universe

In 1998, observations of Type Ia supernovae at great distances showed that the universe’s expansion is accelerating — not slowing as gravity should cause. This acceleration is attributed to dark energy — a form of energy intrinsic to space itself, accounting for about 68% of the universe’s total energy content. Dark energy is even more poorly understood than dark matter; it cannot currently be detected directly.

The future of the universe depends on the relative strengths of gravity (trying to decelerate expansion) and dark energy (trying to accelerate it). Current models suggest three possible fates:

  • Big Freeze (most likely in current models): expansion continues indefinitely; galaxies drift apart; stars use up their fuel; the universe cools towards absolute zero.
  • Big Crunch: gravity eventually overcomes expansion and the universe collapses back to a singularity (requires dark energy to weaken).
  • Big Rip: dark energy strengthens over time, eventually ripping apart all structures — galaxies, then stars, then atoms — as the expansion rate becomes infinite.

Two independent methods give slightly different values for H₀. The Planck satellite’s measurement of the cosmic microwave background gives roughly 67 km/s/Mpc, while distance ladders built from Cepheid variables and Type Ia supernovae give around 73 km/s/Mpc. The gap, called the Hubble tension, is small but stubborn. Resolving it may need new physics — possibly hinting at properties of dark energy not yet captured by the standard cosmological model. For exam purposes the syllabus value of ~70 km/s/Mpc is fine.
exam_tip_html: Calculation questions on Hubble’s law require careful unit management: velocity in km/s, distance in Mpc, \(H_0 = 70\) km/s/Mpc. Always state the formula \(v = H_0 d\) before substituting. For the redshift formula, note that the data sheet provides \(H_0\) — always check if you’re given a slightly different value (68 km/s/Mpc appears in some versions). For extended-response questions on Big Bang evidence, name all three strands (galaxy redshifts, CMB, quasar distribution) and explain each — listing them without explanation earns minimal marks. Always contrast with the Steady State model when evaluating evidence: state what the Steady State predicted and why the observation contradicts it.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Redshift formula: \(\Delta\lambda / \lambda = v/c\). Hubble’s law: \(v = H_0 d\) with \(H_0 \approx 70\) km/s/Mpc. The age of the universe \(\approx 1/H_0 \approx 13.8\) Gyr.
  • Three pieces of Big Bang evidence: galaxy redshifts (expanding universe), CMB at 2.7 K (cooled relic of hot early universe), quasar distribution at high redshift (universe was different in the past). The Steady State model is rejected by all three.
  • Dark matter (27% of energy density) is inferred from galactic rotation curves; dark energy (68%) drives accelerating expansion detected from Type Ia supernovae. Future fates include Big Freeze (most likely), Big Crunch or Big Rip.

practice_questions.text:
A spectral line with a rest wavelength of 400 nm is observed at 410 nm in a distant galaxy. Which one of the following is the recession velocity of the galaxy?
(Speed of light = 3 × 10^5 km/s)
A) 7,500 km/s
B) 75,000 km/s
C) 750 km/s
D) 750,000 km/s
State what is meant by the cosmic microwave background radiation and give its approximate temperature.
practice_questions.marks: The cosmic microwave background (CMB) is thermal radiation that fills the entire universe uniformly, detected at microwave wavelengths [1]. It has a temperature of approximately 2.7 K [1].

practice_questions.text: A galaxy is observed to have a recession velocity of 4,200 km/s. Using Hubble's law with H0 = 70 km/s/Mpc, calculate its distance in Mpc. Show your working.
Explain how observations of galactic rotation curves provide evidence for the existence of dark matter.
practice_questions.marks: Stars at the outer edges of galaxies are observed to orbit at roughly constant speed regardless of distance from the centre [1]. If only visible matter contributed to gravity, orbital speed should decrease with distance (analogous to outer planets in the Solar System) [1]. The constant rotation speed implies a large amount of unseen mass (dark matter) distributed throughout the galactic halo, providing extra gravitational pull at large distances [1].

practice_questions.text: Compare the Big Bang theory and the Steady State theory as models of the universe. In your answer, state what each model predicts and give two pieces of observational evidence that support the Big Bang and contradict the Steady State.
practice_questions.marks:
Big Bang: universe began in an extremely hot, dense state ~13.8 Gyr ago and has been expanding and cooling since [1]. Steady State: universe has always existed; matter is continuously created to maintain constant average density as the universe expands [1].

Evidence for Big Bang / against Steady State:
• CMB: a uniform 2.7 K radiation field permeates the universe, consistent with cooling from a hot Big Bang; Steady State cannot account for this relic radiation [1]
• Quasar distribution: quasars exist predominantly at high redshifts (early universe), showing the universe was different in the past; Steady State requires the universe to look the same at all epochs [1]
(Also credit: galaxy redshifts implying a finite-age expanding universe.)

practice_questions.text:
Celia Ngozi, a postgraduate student at the Caerwyn Observatory in Wales, is giving a public lecture on the fate of the universe. She presents three possible end scenarios: the Big Freeze, the Big Crunch, and the Big Rip.

For each scenario, describe the physical mechanism and current observational constraints. Evaluate which scenario is best supported by current evidence, and explain the role of dark energy and dark matter in determining the ultimate fate of the universe.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Describes all three scenarios correctly (Big Freeze: indefinite expansion, stars die, universe cools; Big Crunch: gravity overcomes expansion, universe collapses; Big Rip: dark energy strengthens, tears apart all structure); links each to gravitational vs dark energy balance; correctly identifies Big Freeze as the scenario most consistent with current data (Type Ia supernovae show accelerating expansion driven by constant dark energy); notes dark matter contributes gravitational attraction but is outweighed by dark energy in current models; dark energy is poorly understood and its behaviour in the far future is unknown, making the Big Rip a genuine possibility if dark energy density increases over time; acknowledges uncertainty.

Secure (3-4): Describes all three scenarios, identifies Big Freeze as currently favoured, mentions role of dark energy; some evaluation of uncertainty.

Developing (1-2): Describes one or two scenarios; limited evaluation; dark matter/dark energy confused or absent.

Emerging (0): Irrelevant or no response.

knowledge_checks.q: A galaxy's spectral line is shifted to a longer wavelength than its rest value. What does this indicate?
options: The galaxy is receding from Earth
The galaxy has a higher surface temperature than the Sun

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is the strongest direct evidence for the Big Bang theory?
options: The Sun's position in the Milky Way
The cosmic microwave background radiation at 2.7 K
The classification of galaxies by Hubble

knowledge_checks.q: Hubble's law states that recession velocity v = H0 × d, where d is distance in Mpc and H0 is approximately _____ km/s/Mpc.
The Steady State model was rejected primarily because it could not explain the existence of the _____ radiation.
Match each cosmological observation to the conclusion it supports.
right: Evidence for dark matter in galactic halos
Evidence for dark energy driving accelerating expansion
Cooled remnant of the hot Big Bang early universe

flashcard_questions.a: Delta-lambda / lambda = v / c, where delta-lambda is the wavelength shift, lambda is the rest wavelength, v is recession velocity, and c is the speed of light.
v = H0 d, where v is recession velocity (km/s), H0 is the Hubble constant (~70 km/s/Mpc), and d is distance in megaparsecs.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the age of the universe?
What is the cosmic microwave background (CMB)?
flashcard_questions.a: Thermal radiation at ~2.7 K filling the universe uniformly in all directions; the cooled afterglow of the hot Big Bang.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the distribution of quasars support the Big Bang over the Steady State model?
flashcard_questions.a: Quasars are mostly at high redshifts (early universe), showing the universe was different in the past. The Steady State requires a universe that looks the same at all times.

flashcard_questions.q: What evidence do galactic rotation curves provide for dark matter?
flashcard_questions.a: Outer stars orbit at unexpectedly constant speed, implying unseen mass (dark matter) in the galactic halo beyond the visible disc.
A mysterious form of energy pervading space that drives the accelerating expansion of the universe, making up about 68% of total energy density.

flashcard_questions.q: What observation in 1998 provided evidence for dark energy?
flashcard_questions.a: Type Ia supernovae at great distances were fainter than expected, showing the universe's expansion is accelerating, not slowing.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Big Freeze scenario?
flashcard_questions.a: Indefinite expansion continues; stars exhaust their fuel; the universe cools towards absolute zero. Currently the most likely scenario.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Steady State theory?
flashcard_questions.a: A model in which the universe is eternal and unchanging, with matter continuously created to fill the gaps as it expands; now rejected by the CMB and quasar evidence.

flashcard_questions.q: If a galaxy has a redshift of delta-lambda/lambda = 0.1, what is its recession velocity?

glossary_terms.definition: The shift of spectral lines to longer (redder) wavelengths in the spectrum of an object moving away from the observer.
The constant H0 in Hubble's law (v = H0 d), approximately 70 km/s/Mpc; relates a galaxy's recession velocity to its distance.
Thermal radiation at approximately 2.7 K that fills the universe uniformly in all directions; the cooled remnant of the hot Big Bang early universe.
A now-rejected model proposing that the universe has always existed and looks the same at all times, with matter continuously created as the universe expands.
Matter that interacts gravitationally but does not emit, absorb or reflect electromagnetic radiation, inferred from galactic rotation curves; ~27% of the universe's energy density.
A mysterious energy intrinsic to space that drives the accelerating expansion of the universe, accounting for approximately 68% of its total energy density.
The scenario in which the universe expands indefinitely, stars exhaust their fuel, and the universe cools towards absolute zero; the most likely outcome under current models.
The scenario in which gravity eventually overcomes expansion and the universe collapses back to a singularity.
The scenario in which dark energy strengthens over time, eventually ripping apart all matter at all scales as expansion becomes infinite.

items.title: TIMELAPSE OF THE FUTURE: A Journey to the End of Time (4K)
items.description: From today through to the Big Freeze trillions of years hence — visualises the three possible fates of the universe (Big Freeze, Big Rip, Big Crunch) using the latest cosmological data.

items.title: What is Dark Matter and Dark Energy?
items.description: Clear explanation of galactic rotation curves as evidence for dark matter, and Type Ia supernovae as evidence for dark energy driving accelerating expansion.

items.title: Why Black Holes Could Delete The Universe — The Information Paradox
items.description: Explores the tension between black hole thermodynamics and quantum mechanics — a cutting-edge extension of the Big Bang and dark energy questions that remain unsolved.

items.title: Contact (1997)
items.description: The film opens with a spectacular zoom out from Earth through the observable universe — the exact journey described by Hubble's law and the cosmic distance ladder.

items.title: Black Holes: The Edge of All We Know (2021)
items.description: Filming the black hole at the heart of a distant galaxy is itself a window into the early universe — quasars at high redshift are the same class of object imaged by the EHT team.

items.title: ESA: Planck Mission — Mapping the CMB
items.description: ESA's overview of the Planck satellite, which produced the most precise map of the cosmic microwave background — key evidence for the Big Bang discussed in this lesson.
